n0001.title: On the Origin of Species
n0001.gist: Darwin argues that all species descend with modification from common ancestors through natural selection acting on inherited variation in the struggle for existence.
n0001.sourceHeading: The Project Gutenberg eBook of On the Origin of Species, by Charles Darwin

n0002.title: Front Matter and Table of Contents
n0002.gist: The Gutenberg edition front matter presents the book's title, epigraphs, and a detailed chapter-by-chapter contents list.

n0003.title: Publication Details
n0003.gist: The ebook lists available Gutenberg editions of Darwin's work.

n0009.title: Title Page
n0009.gist: The title page names the book and its author, Charles Darwin.

n0014.title: Epigraphs and Dedication
n0014.gist: Darwin prefaces the work with quotations from Whewell and Bacon and dates it from Down, Kent.

n0021.title: Contents
n0021.gist: A heading introduces the detailed table of contents.

n0025.title: Detailed Chapter Summaries
n0025.gist: Each of the fourteen chapters is previewed with a list of its main topics.

n0055.title: Introduction
n0055.gist: Darwin explains how years of observation, aided by Wallace's parallel work, led him to publish an abstract arguing that species are not immutable but descend with modification, mainly through natural selection.

n0056.title: Origin of the Work
n0056.gist: Darwin recounts his long study since the Beagle voyage and his decision to publish after receiving Wallace's similar essay.

n0065.title: Outline of the Argument
n0065.gist: Darwin previews how domestic variation, struggle for existence, and natural selection together explain the origin of species.

n0072.title: Variation Under Domestication and Nature
n0072.gist: Comparing pigeons and other domestic breeds with wild species, Darwin shows that heritable variation, shaped by man's selection, closely parallels the variability found among species in nature.

n0073.title: Causes and Laws of Variability
n0073.gist: Domestic organisms vary more than wild ones because of altered conditions of life, with inheritance, correlation of growth, and reversion governing how variations spread.

n0090.title: Pigeon Breeds and Their Common Origin
n0090.gist: Despite their extreme diversity, all domestic pigeon breeds are shown to descend from the single wild rock-pigeon.

n0102.title: Selection by Man
n0102.gist: Methodical and unconscious selection by breeders, acting on tiny individual differences over generations, has produced all our distinct domestic races.

n0123.title: Summary of Domestic Variation
n0123.gist: Variability, inheritance, and accumulated selection together explain the origin of domestic races.

n0125.title: CHAPTER II. VARIATION UNDER NATURE.
n0125.gist: Wild species show the same graded variability as domestic ones, and species of the largest, most widespread genera vary the most, blurring the line between varieties and species.

n0151.title: Struggle and Natural Selection
n0151.gist: Because every organism tends to multiply faster than resources allow, a constant struggle for existence lets natural selection preserve favorable variations, driving divergence, extinction, and adaptation.

n0152.title: CHAPTER III. STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE.
n0152.gist: All organisms tend to increase geometrically, so a universal struggle for existence checks their numbers and sets the stage for selection.

n0182.title: Natural Selection Defined
n0182.gist: Natural selection is the preservation of favorable and rejection of injurious variations in the struggle for life.

n0194.title: Sexual Selection
n0194.gist: Competition among males for mates produces weapons, ornaments, and songs through a milder form of selection.

n0198.title: Illustrations of Natural Selection
n0198.gist: Hypothetical cases of wolves, flowers, and bees show how natural selection could gradually build complex adaptations.

n0205.title: Intercrossing and Favourable Circumstances
n0205.gist: Occasional crossing between individuals, along with isolation and large numbers, favors the work of natural selection.

n0224.title: Extinction and Divergence of Character
n0224.gist: Natural selection drives less-favored forms extinct while favoring ever more divergent descendants, producing the branching tree of life.

n0259.title: Laws of Variation and Difficulties on Theory
n0259.gist: Darwin explains variability through use, disuse, and correlated growth, then confronts and answers the gravest objections to natural selection, including the evolution of complex organs like the eye.

n0260.title: Use, Disuse, and Correlation of Growth
n0260.gist: Habitual use or disuse of organs, along with correlated growth, shapes variation independent of direct selection.

n0289.title: Variability of Specific and Sexual Characters
n0289.gist: Traits that distinguish species vary more than generic ones, and secondary sexual characters are especially variable, reflecting recent and ongoing modification.

n0314.title: CHAPTER VI. DIFFICULTIES ON THEORY.
n0314.gist: Darwin lists the chief objections to his theory, including the rarity of transitional forms and the origin of complex organs and instincts.

n0327.title: Transitions in Habits and Structure
n0327.gist: Many living species show intermediate habits, showing that structures like wings could evolve gradually from ordinary organs.

n0348.title: Organs of Extreme Perfection
n0348.gist: Even an organ as complex as the eye could evolve through numerous small useful gradations, as seen in graded eye structures across living animals.

n0360.title: Organs of Small Importance and Unity of Type
n0360.gist: Trivial structures and inherited but now-useless features are explained by correlation and inheritance rather than direct utility, unifying structure and conditions of existence.

n0383.title: Instinct and Hybridism
n0383.gist: Instincts, however marvelous, can be built by natural selection from small variations just as bodily structures are, while the sterility of species crosses proves to be an incidental effect of divergence rather than a special barrier.

n0384.title: Instinct and Its Origin
n0384.gist: Instincts resemble inherited habits and vary like bodily structures, allowing natural selection to shape them gradually.

n0397.title: Domestic and Natural Instincts Compared
n0397.gist: Instincts of domestic animals such as pointing dogs show the same kind of heritable variation as wild instincts like the cuckoo's parasitism.

n0413.title: The Hive-Bee's Cell-Making Instinct
n0413.gist: The bee's geometrically perfect comb can be explained as the outcome of simple instincts for economizing wax, refined by selection.

n0436.title: Neuter Insects and Summary of Instinct
n0436.gist: Sterile worker castes, seemingly fatal to the theory, are explained by selection acting on the fertile parents that produce them.

n0440.title: CHAPTER VIII. HYBRIDISM.
n0440.gist: The sterility of species crosses and the fertility of variety crosses are shown to grade into each other rather than form an absolute divide.

n0475.title: Causes of Sterility and Fertility Compared
n0475.gist: Sterility parallels the disturbance caused by unnatural conditions, and hybrids and mongrels resemble each other closely apart from fertility.

n0498.title: Geological Record and Succession
n0498.gist: The fossil record's extreme incompleteness explains the absence of countless transitional forms, while the actual succession of fossils—gradual appearance, extinction, and increasing modification—matches what descent with modification predicts.

n0499.title: The Imperfection of the Geological Record
n0499.gist: Vast unrecorded time, sparse fossilization, and intermittent deposition explain why intermediate forms are rarely preserved.

n0517.title: Poorness of Collections and Intermittent Formations
n0517.gist: Our fossil collections are fragmentary, and formations accumulate only during subsidence, leaving huge gaps in the record.

n0551.title: Sudden Appearance of Species Groups
n0551.gist: Apparently abrupt appearances of whole groups, even in the earliest strata, reflect gaps in exploration and record rather than sudden creation.

n0555.title: CHAPTER X. GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION.
n0555.gist: New species appear slowly and never reappear once extinct, matching the predictions of gradual modification and extinction.
n0555.sourceHeading: CHAPTER X. ON THE GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF ORGANIC BEINGS.

n0573.title: Affinities, Development, and Summary
n0573.gist: Extinct forms bridge living groups, ancient life is generally less developed, and the same types persist within the same regions—facts all explained by inherited descent.

n0609.title: Geographic Distribution
n0609.gist: The distribution of species across barriers, oceans, and islands, along with the effects of past climate change, shows that living things have spread from single centers of origin and diversified through migration and modification rather than independent creation.

n0610.title: Barriers and Centres of Creation
n0610.gist: Similar climates house very different species while barriers like oceans mark sharp boundaries, implying each species arose once and spread from a single area.

n0626.title: Means of Dispersal
n0626.gist: Seeds and small organisms can cross oceans via currents, floating debris, and birds, explaining wide but not unlimited distribution.

n0635.title: Dispersal During the Glacial Period
n0635.gist: A simultaneous worldwide cooling explains why the same or related alpine and arctic species occur on separated mountains and continents.

n0661.title: Fresh-Water and Oceanic Island Life
n0661.gist: Fresh-water species disperse surprisingly widely via birds and floods, while oceanic islands host few but often endemic species related to the nearest mainland.

n0685.title: Summary of Distribution
n0685.gist: Migration with subsequent modification from a nearest source explains the parallel patterns of distribution across time and space.

n0695.title: Classification and Conclusion
n0695.gist: Natural classification, embryology, and rudimentary organs all reveal descent with modification, and Darwin closes by weighing the theory's remaining difficulties against the vast body of evidence it explains.

n0696.title: Principles of Classification
n0696.gist: Naturalists' groups-within-groups and their rules of classification reflect genealogical descent rather than an arbitrary or purely practical scheme.

n0727.title: Morphology and Embryology
n0727.gist: Shared skeletal patterns and embryonic resemblances across species are explained by inheritance from common ancestors modified at later life stages.

n0750.title: Rudimentary Organs and Chapter Summary
n0750.gist: Useless vestigial organs, otherwise inexplicable, are natural remnants of once-functional structures inherited from ancestors.

n0766.title: Recapitulation of Difficulties
n0766.gist: Darwin restates the main objections—hybrid sterility, gaps in distribution and the fossil record—and his answers to each.

n0779.title: Recapitulation of the Evidence
n0779.gist: Darwin reviews how variation, selection, geology, distribution, classification, and embryology together support descent with modification.

n0803.title: Concluding Remarks
n0803.gist: Darwin closes by predicting a revolution in natural history and reflecting on the grandeur of life's evolution from simple beginnings.
